newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia government MP hits Howard's land plan.
newsitem.headline: Australia government MP hits Howard's land plan.

text.p: An influential Australian government politician on Monday criticised Prime Minister John Howard's planned compromise to end a national row over conflicting land claims between Aborigines and farmers.

Liberal Party backbencher Wilson Tuckey said Howard's compromise did not give farmers, who say the row is damaging their business, enough certainty over their rights to land leased from the government.
Howard summoned state and territory leaders to Canberra on Monday for an emergency summit to discuss the problem, which has pitted farmers against Aborigines and split political allies.
"The document that I have seen certainly doesn't provide absolute certainty for titleholders throughout Australia," said Tuckey, who heads Howard's special backbench committee on Aboriginal affairs.
Tuckey told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio his committee was demanding "absolute certainty" for farmers.

"We find it, in fact, ludicrous that a certain group of people have the right to abstract other people in their ownership, development, or peaceful occupancy of land on the grounds that they've made a claim for it," he said, adding he had only seen an unofficial version of Howard's plan.

Howard is seeking backing for his 10-point compromise deal, the key elements of which include confirming farmers' rights over their properties, but guaranteeing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.
The plan has been criticised by Aborigines, farmers and the National Party, the junior member in Howard's ruling Liberal-National coalition.
Miners and farmers say uncertainty has crippled valuable primary industries since the High Court ruled in December that Aborigines had rights to government land leased to farmers.

But the court, in what is known as the Wik decision, did not specify those rights. Howard has said 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles) could be claimed by Aborigines under native title land laws.
